title: 3 Ways to Make Sure Every Loss Becomes a Win
author: Joel Salinas
summary: Joel Salinas argues that mission-driven teams, especially nonprofits and churches, cannot afford to waste failure and must build rhythms that turn losses into learning. He illustrates with the Post-it Note, which began as 3M's failed attempt at a strong adhesive and became a major product line because colleagues revisited it with better questions. He explains why the stakes are higher for organizations with thin margins, where silence after a failed pilot means losing twice. He offers three practices: debrief everything, name failures openly, and convert lessons into checklists and if/then plans. A short loss-to-learning checklist and a TL;DR close the piece. The advice is general and anecdotal rather than evidence-based, but it is a clear, usable team practice.
points: Failure is only a loss if the team does not learn from it, and learning has to be designed in because teams do not drift into it.
Debriefing only after failures makes reflection reactive; debriefing after every launch, retreat or campaign makes it a norm.
Leaders who name what did not go as planned build trust and show new staff what risk looks like, and teams will not do this unless leaders model it first.
Lessons need to become checklists, process tweaks or if/then plans so reflection produces changed behavior.
The Post-it Note story shows that a failure revisited with curiosity can become a successful product.
quotes: Most nonprofit and church leaders I know aren’t afraid to take risks. They’re afraid the risks won’t be worth it. When resources are tight and people are counting on you, it’s tempting to play it safe, especially after a failed initiative, a missed grant, or a burned-out team member.
What made the difference? The company didn’t bury the failure, they revisited it. They asked better questions. They stayed curious.
If a failed pilot program or dropped initiative leads to silence or shutdown, we lose twice: once in the outcome, and again in the opportunity to learn.
Most teams only debrief when something goes wrong. But if we want learning to be a norm, not a reaction, we need to normalize reflection across the board.
In healthy cultures, naming what didn’t work isn’t a threat; it’s a gift. It builds trust. It teaches new staff what risk looks like. It makes senior leaders more human.

Make it a norm to say, “Here’s where this didn’t go as planned, and here’s what we’re seeing now because of it.” If leaders don’t model this, teams won’t either. Courageous clarity creates strategic momentum.
